chem_ocra.7.0.summary: Oxidation and reduction, collectively known as redox reactions, can be defined through the transfer of oxygen or electrons between chemical species. Understanding these processes at a particulate level using half-equations and oxidation state changes is essential for mastering chemical reactivity, extraction of metals, and electrolysis in OCR GCSE Chemistry.

core.p: Chemical reactions often involve the transfer of particles from one reactant to another. Redox is a portmanteau term standing for reduction-oxidation, meaning both processes always happen simultaneously.
bullets: Reduction and oxidation are inextricably linked; you cannot have one without the other.
In any redox reaction, if one substance is oxidised, another substance must be reduced.
Historical definitions relied purely on the addition and removal of oxygen atoms.
Modern electronic definitions rely on the transfer of electrons between atoms, ions, or molecules.

callouts.p: A reaction in which both reduction and oxidation occur simultaneously, involving the transfer of oxygen or electrons.

core.h: Definition 1: Redox in Terms of Oxygen
core.p: The earliest definition of redox is based on oxygen gas. This is most commonly seen in metal extraction where metal oxides are heated with carbon.
bullets: **Oxidation** is the **gain of oxygen** by a substance.
**Reduction** is the **loss of oxygen** from a substance.
Example: Copper(II) oxide reacting with hydrogen gas forms copper and water.
Equation: CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O
In this reaction, CuO is reduced to Cu, while H2 is oxidised to H2O.

callouts.p: OIL RIG does not apply directly to oxygen definitions; instead use RIG (Reduction Is Gain of oxygen) and OAO (Oxidation Is Addition of oxygen).

fig.cap: Diagram showing the loss of oxygen from copper oxide and gain of oxygen by hydrogen during reduction and oxidation.

core.h: Definition 2: Redox in Terms of Electrons (OIL RIG)
core.p: As chemistry advanced, scientists realised redox applies to reactions without oxygen. The modern electronic definition covers all chemical interactions.
bullets: **OIL RIG**: **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss (of electrons), **R**eduction **I**s **G**ain (of electrons).
When an atom or ion loses negative electrons, its overall electrical charge increases (becomes more positive).
When an atom or ion gains negative electrons, its overall electrical charge decreases (becomes more negative).
This definition is universal and applies to ionic bonding, displacement, and electrolysis.

callouts.p: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

core.p: Agents are the chemical species that cause other substances to undergo oxidation or reduction while experiencing the opposite process themselves.
bullets: An **oxidising agent** brings about oxidation by **accepting electrons** (it gets reduced itself).
A **reducing agent** brings about reduction by **donating electrons** (it gets oxidised itself).
In terms of oxygen, the oxidising agent gives away its oxygen, while the reducing agent takes the oxygen.
Fluorine and chlorine are powerful oxidising agents; carbon and hydrogen are common reducing agents.

callouts.p: Students often confuse the substance being oxidised with the oxidising agent. Remember: the oxidising agent itself is reduced!

core.p: Half-equations show explicitly how electrons are transferred during a reaction. An oxidation half-equation always features electrons written on the product side.
bullets: Oxidation half-equation template: Atom -> Ion + e-
Example for magnesium forming magnesium ions: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-
Magnesium metal loses two electrons to form a stable Mg2+ ion.
The electrons appear on the right side because they are products of the oxidation step.

callouts.p: Always balance the atoms first, then add electrons to balance the total electrical charges on both sides.

core.p: Reduction half-equations show species gaining electrons. The electrons must appear on the reactant side because they are consumed in the process.
bullets: Reduction half-equation template: Ion + e- -> Atom or lower-charged ion
Example for chlorine gas forming chloride ions: Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-
Example for copper ions forming copper atoms: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu
The electrons are written on the left side because they are reactants added to the species.

callouts.p: Reduction = electrons on Left (Reactants). Oxidation = electrons on Right (Products).

core.h: Combining Half-Equations to Form Ionic Equations
core.p: To form an overall ionic equation for a redox process, the oxidation and reduction half-equations must be combined by balancing the number of electrons transferred.
bullets: Ensure the number of electrons lost in oxidation equals the number of electrons gained in reduction.
Add the reactant sides together and the product sides together.
Cancel out any electrons that appear on both sides of the combined equation.
This method is frequently used in metal displacement and electrolysis questions.

callouts.p: If electrons do not match in number, multiply one or both half-equations by whole numbers before adding.

core.p: When a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt, electrons are transferred directly between the metal atoms and metal ions.
bullets: Example: Zinc added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
Overall equation: Zn(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> ZnSO4(aq) + Cu(s)
Ionic equation: Zn(s) + Cu2+(aq) -> Zn2+(aq) + Cu(s)
Zinc atoms are oxidised: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-
Copper ions are reduced: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu

callouts.p: Sulfate ions (SO4 2-) do not change during displacement; they are spectator ions and are omitted from ionic equations.

fig.cap: Diagram illustrating electron transfer from solid zinc atoms to copper ions in solution during displacement.

core.p: Halogens follow a reactivity trend down Group 7, where more reactive halogens displace less reactive halide ions from aqueous solutions in a redox process.
bullets: Reactivity of halogens decreases down the group: Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
Example: Chlorine gas added to potassium bromide solution.
Ionic equation: Cl2(aq) + 2Br-(aq) -> 2Cl-(aq) + Br2(aq)
Bromide ions are oxidised (lose electrons): 2Br- -> Br2 + 2e-
Chlorine molecules are reduced (gain electrons): Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Cl-

callouts.p: Be careful with nomenclature: 'chlorine' is Cl2, whereas 'chloride' is the ion Cl-. Examiners penalise missing subscripts.

core.p: Metals less reactive than carbon, such as iron, are extracted from their ores in a blast furnace by heating the metal oxide with carbon or carbon monoxide.
bullets: Equation: 2Fe2O3 + 3C -> 4Fe + 3CO2
Iron(III) oxide loses oxygen, so it is **reduced** to iron metal.
Carbon gains oxygen, so it is **oxidised** to carbon dioxide.
Carbon acts as the reducing agent in this industrial metallurgical process.

callouts.p: Carbon can only reduce oxides of metals less reactive than carbon. Metals above carbon in the reactivity series require electrolysis.

core.p: Electrolysis involves passing an electrical current through an ionic compound (molten or in solution), forcing redox reactions to occur at the electrodes.
bullets: At the **cathode** (negative electrode), positive ions gain electrons. Therefore, reduction always occurs at the cathode.
At the **anode** (positive electrode), negative ions lose electrons. Therefore, oxidation always occurs at the anode.
Mnemonic: **CR**O**P** (**C**athode **R**eduction, **O**xidation **P**ositive? Or better: **LEO says GER** at electrodes).
Example during molten NaCl electrolysis: Na+ + e- -> Na (reduction at cathode); 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e- (oxidation at anode).

callouts.p: Cathode = Reduction (gain of electrons). Anode = Oxidation (loss of electrons).

analogy.p: Imagine a classroom where students trade money. A student who gives away a ten-pound note is losing wealth (Oxidation Is Loss), while the student receiving the ten-pound note is gaining wealth (Reduction Is Gain). Where the analogy breaks down is that chemical reduction and oxidation always involve electrons, and the total number of electrons in the universe remains conserved, whereas money can be spent on external items.

terms.d: A chemical reaction in which reduction and oxidation occur simultaneously.
The gain of oxygen or loss of electrons by a substance.
The loss of oxygen or gain of electrons by a substance.
A substance that oxidises another substance by accepting electrons; it gets reduced itself.
A substance that reduces another substance by donating electrons; it gets oxidised itself.
An equation showing either oxidation or reduction with explicit inclusion of electrons.
A chemical equation that shows reacting ions, omitting spectator ions.
A reaction where a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound.
The negative electrode in electrolysis where reduction takes place.
The positive electrode in electrolysis where oxidation takes place.
An ion that does not change or take part in the chemical reaction.
The breakdown of an ionic substance using electricity.

mistakes.w: Saying oxidation is the loss of hydrogen.
mistakes.r: OCR GCSE expects oxygen or electron definitions only at this tier.

mistakes.w: Writing electrons on the wrong side of half-equations.
mistakes.r: Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation puts electrons on the product side; Reduction puts electrons on the reactant side.

mistakes.w: Stating that the oxidising agent is the substance that gets oxidised.
mistakes.r: The oxidising agent causes oxidation in others while being reduced itself.

mistakes.w: Forgetting state symbols in ionic equations.
mistakes.r: State symbols like (aq), (s), (g) are frequently required in OCR mark schemes.
Only include the species directly gaining or losing electrons.

mistakes.w: Confusing halide ions with halogen molecules.
mistakes.r: Cl- is a chloride ion; Cl2 is a chlorine molecule.

mistakes.w: Saying reduction happens at the anode.
mistakes.r: Reduction always occurs at the cathode.

exam.q: Define oxidation in terms of electrons.
model: Loss of electrons

exam.q: Explain which species is reduced in the reaction: CuO + H2 -> Cu + H2O
model: CuO / copper oxide is reduced
Because it loses oxygen
exam.tip: Always state both the chemical name/formula and the reason.

exam.q: Write the half-equation for the oxidation of magnesium atoms to magnesium ions.
model: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e-
(Award 1 mark for correct formulas, 1 mark for correct balancing and electrons)
exam.tip: Check charges carefully: Mg2+ needs 2 electrons on the product side.

exam.q: Identify the oxidising agent in the reaction: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu
model: Cu2+ / copper ions
exam.tip: The oxidising agent gets reduced (gains electrons).

exam.q: Explain why the reaction between zinc and copper sulfate is a redox reaction.
model: Zinc is oxidised because it loses electrons (or forms Zn2+)
Copper ions are reduced because they gain electrons (or form Cu)
Both oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously
exam.tip: Structure your answer by identifying what happens to each species separately.

exam.q: Write the reduction half-equation for chlorine gas forming chloride ions.
model: (1 mark for reactants/products, 1 mark for balancing electrons)

exam.q: State what happens at the anode during electrolysis in terms of electrons.
model: Loss of electrons (oxidation)

exam.q: In the extraction of iron, iron(III) oxide reacts with carbon. Write the balanced equation and state which substance is the reducing agent.
model: 2Fe2O3 + 3C -> 4Fe + 3CO2
Carbon / C
Because carbon gains oxygen (or causes reduction of iron oxide)
exam.tip: Make sure equation balancing coefficients are correct.

exam.q: A student adds bromine water to potassium iodide solution. State the colour change observed and explain why this is a displacement and redox reaction.
model: Colour changes from orange/brown to brown/violet (iodine produced)
Bromine is more reactive than iodine
Bromine gains electrons to form bromide ions (reduced)
Iodide ions lose electrons to form iodine (oxidised)
exam.tip: Mention both observational changes and electron transfer.

worked.q: Construct the overall ionic equation for the reaction between magnesium and iron(II) sulfate solution, and identify the species oxidised.
steps: Step 1: Write the full word or symbol equation: Mg + FeSO4 -> MgSO4 + Fe
Step 2: Convert into an ionic equation by splitting aqueous ionic compounds: Mg(s) + Fe2+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq) -> Mg2+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq) + Fe(s)
Step 3: Remove spectator ions (SO4 2-): Mg(s) + Fe2+(aq) -> Mg2+(aq) + Fe(s)
Step 4: Identify oxidation: Magnesium atoms lose electrons to form Mg2+, so magnesium is oxidised.
worked.ans: Ionic equation: Mg(s) + Fe2+(aq) -> Mg2+(aq) + Fe(s). Species oxidised: Magnesium (Mg).

worked.q: Write the two half-equations for the reaction between zinc and copper ions, and show how they combine.
steps: Step 1: Write oxidation half-equation for zinc: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-
Step 2: Write reduction half-equation for copper ions: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu
Step 3: Check electron numbers (both have 2e-, so they balance perfectly).
Step 4: Add reactants and products together, cancelling electrons: Zn + Cu2+ + 2e- -> Zn2+ + Cu + 2e- becomes Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu
worked.ans: Oxidation: Zn -> Zn2+ + 2e-. Reduction: Cu2+ + 2e- -> Cu. Combined: Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu.

chem_ocra.7.2.summary: Neutralisation is the chemical reaction between an acid and a base (or alkali) producing a salt and water, fundamentally driven by the combination of hydrogen and hydroxide ions to form water. This section explores the underlying ionic equations that prove why different neutralisations share the exact same core process, alongside the practical techniques of PAG C7 for preparing pure, dry salt crystals.

core.p: Neutralisation is the reaction between hydrogen ions from an acid and hydroxide ions from an alkali to produce water. When an acid reacts with a base, the pH moves closer to 7 as the excess hydrogen ions are removed from the solution.
bullets: Acids produce hydrogen ions (H+) in aqueous solution.
Alkalis produce hydroxide ions (OH-) in aqueous solution.
General word equation: Acid + Base -> Salt + Water (+ Carbon dioxide if a carbonate is used).
The universal chemical heart of all neutralisations is the formation of water molecules.

callouts.p: The reaction between hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions to form water.
H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l) is the ionic equation for all acid-alkali neutralisations.

core.p: An ionic equation focuses only on the reacting particles that undergo a chemical change, omitting spectator ions which remain unchanged in solution. For a neutralisation reaction, spectator ions are removed to reveal the core ionic change.
bullets: Step 1: Write the balanced full chemical equation with state symbols.
Step 2: Split all aqueous ionic compounds into their respective constituent ions.
Step 3: Cancel out spectator ions that appear identically on both sides of the equation.
Step 4: Rewrite the remaining species as the final ionic equation.

callouts.p: Always include (aq), (s), (l), and (g) when explicitly requested by mark schemes in ionic equations.

fig.cap: Visualising spectator ions vs reacting ions in a neutralisation reaction between HCl and NaOH.

core.h: Required Practical C7: Making Soluble Salts
core.p: PAG C7 involves reacting an acid with an insoluble base (such as copper oxide) to prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt. Excess solid is added to ensure all the acid reacts completely.
bullets: Step 1: Add excess insoluble base to warm dilute acid in a beaker until no more reacts (solid sits at the bottom).
Step 2: Filter the mixture using filter paper and a funnel to remove the unreacted excess solid.
Step 3: Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin over a water bath until crystals start to form (crystallisation point).
Step 4: Leave the solution to cool and crystallise fully, then pat the dry crystals with filter paper.

callouts.p: Adding excess ensures all acid is used up so the final salt solution is not contaminated by leftover acidic hydrogen ions.

core.p: When making a soluble salt from an acid and a soluble alkali (like sodium hydroxide), titration must be used because both reactants are liquids and there is no visual excess solid to filter off.
bullets: Step 1: Use a pipette to measure a fixed volume of alkali into a conical flask.
Step 2: Add a few drops of a suitable indicator (phenolphthalein or methyl orange).
Step 3: Add acid from a burette, swirling constantly, until the indicator changes colour permanently at the endpoint.
Step 4: Repeat without indicator using the exact volume of acid found to get a pure salt solution, then evaporate.

callouts.p: Never use universal indicator in titrations because its colour change is gradual (a continuous spectrum), making it impossible to spot a sharp endpoint.

core.p: Choosing the correct indicator is essential for identifying the precise neutralisation point during titrations. Phenolphthalein and methyl orange are the standard choices in GCSE chemistry.
bullets: Phenolphthalein is pink in alkaline solutions and colourless in acidic solutions.
Methyl orange is yellow in alkaline solutions and red in acidic solutions.
At the exact point of neutralisation, the indicator shows a distinct intermediate or sharp transition colour.
Indicator volume must be kept small (1-2 drops) so it does not act as an acid and alter titration results.

core.p: When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate, neutralisation occurs alongside effervescence due to carbon dioxide gas production. The ionic equation includes the carbonate ion reacting with hydrogen ions.
bullets: General equation: Acid + Metal Carbonate -> Salt + Water + Carbon dioxide.
Ionic equation for carbonate neutralisation: 2H+(aq) + CO32-(aq) -> H2O(l) + CO2(g).
Observation: Effervescence/bubbling and solid carbonate disappearing as it reacts.
Limewater can be used to test the evolved gas, turning milky/cloudy due to insoluble calcium carbonate formation.

callouts.p: Remember that carbonate is CO32-, so it requires two H+ ions to form one molecule of water and one of carbon dioxide.

core.p: Reactive metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with acids in a redox neutralisation process producing a salt and hydrogen gas.
bullets: General equation: Acid + Metal -> Salt + Hydrogen.
Ionic equation: Mg(s) + 2H+(aq) -> Mg2+(aq) + H2(g).
Observations: Effervescence of hydrogen gas and metal dissolving.
Unreactive metals like copper, silver, and gold do not react with dilute acids.

core.p: Spectator ions are ions that are present in the reaction mixture but do not participate in the chemical change. They remain dissolved in the aqueous solution throughout the reaction.
bullets: In the reaction between HCl and NaOH, Na+ and Cl- are spectator ions.
They appear on both the reactant and product sides of the full ionic equation.
Removing spectator ions isolates the fundamental chemical process occurring in the system.
Allows comparison of neutralisation enthalpy changes across different strong acids and alkalis.

core.p: Neutralisation reactions are exothermic, meaning they release thermal energy to the surroundings. The temperature of the reaction mixture increases as neutralisation proceeds.
bullets: Energy is released when bonds form, specifically when H+ and OH- combine to form H2O.
The enthalpy change of neutralisation for strong acids and strong alkalis is roughly constant (~ -57 kJ/mol).
Polyprotic acids (like H2SO4) release more energy per mole of acid because they provide more H+ ions.
Polystyrene cups and lids are used in calorimetry experiments to minimise heat loss to the surroundings.

core.p: Salts are ionic compounds formed when the hydrogen ions in an acid are replaced by metal ions or ammonium ions. The name of the salt depends on the parent acid used.
bullets: Hydrochloric acid produces chloride salts (e.g., NaCl, CuCl2).
Sulfuric acid produces sulfate salts (e.g., Na2SO4, CuSO4).
Nitric acid produces nitrate salts (e.g., KNO3, Mg(NO3)2).
Formula construction requires balancing the charges of the positive metal ion and negative non-metal/polyatomic ion.

core.p: Crystallisation is a purification technique used to obtain pure, dry crystals of a soluble salt from its solution after neutralisation.
bullets: Heat the solution gently to evaporate water and increase concentration.
Stop heating when crystals start to form around the edge of the basin (the saturation point).
Allow the basin to cool slowly at room temperature so larger, well-formed crystals grow.
Filter or decant remaining liquid, then dry crystals gently between sheets of filter paper.

callouts.p: Do not heat to complete dryness with a direct Bunsen burner flame, as water of crystallisation may be driven off or hydrated salts can spit/decompose.

core.p: Depending on whether the base is soluble or insoluble, different laboratory methods are required to prepare a pure dry salt sample safely and efficiently.
bullets: Insoluble base (metal oxide, hydroxide, carbonate): Excess solid method with filtration and crystallisation.
Soluble base/alkali (soluble metal hydroxide/ammonia): Titration method using an indicator, followed by crystallisation without indicator.
Metals: Excess metal method with filtration (only for moderately reactive metals like zinc, iron, magnesium).
Always confirm complete reaction when using solids by noting when excess solid stops dissolving.

analogy.t: The Lock and Key Dance Party
analogy.p: Imagine a crowded dance floor where acidic hydrogen ions (aggressive solo dancers wearing red hats, H+) and alkaline hydroxide ions (blue hats, OH-) desperately want to pair up. When they find each other, they immediately hug tightly to form a stable couple dancing in place (water, H2O). Other ions like sodium (Na+) and chloride (Cl-) are just wallflowers standing on the edge watching; they don't participate in the dance and are the spectator ions. Where it breaks down: real ions are floating freely in an aqueous solution surrounded by water molecules, not moving around a physical dance floor looking for partners.

terms.d: The reaction between hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions to form water, or more broadly, the reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water.
An equation that shows only the reacting ions that undergo a change during a chemical reaction, omitting spectator ions.
An ion that is present in a reaction mixture but does not take part in the chemical reaction.
An ionic compound formed when the hydrogen ions in an acid are replaced by metal ions or ammonium ions.
A substance that reacts with an acid to neutralise it, including metal oxides, metal hydroxides, and metal carbonates.
A soluble base that dissolves in water to produce hydroxide ions (OH-).
An analytical volumetric technique used to find the exact volume of solution needed to react completely with another solution.
The point in a titration where the indicator changes colour, signalling that neutralisation is complete.
The process by which crystals form as a solution cools or evaporates, used to purify soluble salts.
A chemical process that releases thermal energy to the surroundings, causing temperature to rise.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether it is in an acidic or alkaline solution.
The liquid that passes through filter paper during filtration, separating it from the residue.

mistakes.w: Writing H3O+ instead of H+ in ionic equations at GCSE level.
mistakes.r: OCR mark schemes expect H+(aq) for hydrogen ions.

mistakes.w: Including spectator ions in the ionic equation for neutralisation.
mistakes.r: Spectator ions must be cancelled out; the ionic equation is strictly H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l).
Universal indicator has no sharp colour change; phenolphthalein or methyl orange must be used.

mistakes.w: Stating that neutralisation produces a neutral solution (pH 7) always.
mistakes.r: Neutralisation produces a salt and water; if a strong acid is neutralised by a weak alkali, the resulting salt solution may be acidic.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to state that excess solid is added when preparing a salt from an insoluble base.
mistakes.r: You must specify adding 'excess' solid so all acid is used up.

mistakes.w: Saying salt crystals are dried by heating strongly with a Bunsen burner.
mistakes.r: Crystals are dried by patting with filter paper or leaving in a warm drying oven to prevent decomposition.

mistakes.w: Omitting state symbols in ionic equations when requested.
mistakes.r: Always include (aq), (s), (l), (g) when spec or mark scheme asks for ionic equations with state symbols.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the neutralisation reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.
model: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)
exam.tip: Memorise this exact equation; it is worth 1 mark in almost every exam paper.

exam.q: Explain why excess copper oxide is added when preparing copper sulfate crystals.
model: To ensure all the sulfuric acid reacts completely
So that the final salt solution is not contaminated by unreacted acid
exam.tip: Always link excess solid to using up all the acid completely.

exam.q: Describe how to obtain pure, dry crystals of magnesium sulfate from a mixture of magnesium sulfate solution.
model: Heat the solution in an evaporating basin over a water bath
Heat until crystals begin to form around the edge (crystallisation point)
Leave the solution to cool and allow crystals to form fully
Filter or blot the crystals dry using filter paper
exam.tip: Mention heating to saturation, cooling for crystal growth, and drying.

exam.q: Explain why universal indicator is unsuitable for use in a titration.
model: Universal indicator gives a continuous range of colours depending on pH
It does not have a sharp colour change, making it impossible to spot the exact endpoint
exam.tip: Contrast with single indicators like phenolphthalein which show a sharp, sudden change.

exam.q: Write the balanced ionic equation for the reaction of dilute nitric acid with calcium carbonate.
model: 2H+(aq) + CaCO3(s) -> Ca2+(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g) OR 2H+(aq) + CO32-(aq) -> H2O(l) + CO2(g)
exam.tip: Calcium carbonate is solid, so keep (s) in the ionic equation as it does not dissolve completely as independent ions.

exam.q: Define a spectator ion in the context of chemical reactions.
model: An ion that does not change or take part in the chemical reaction

exam.q: State the colour change of phenolphthalein indicator when added to an alkali being titrated with an acid.
model: Starts pink in the alkali
Turns colourless at the endpoint when neutralised by the acid
exam.tip: Specify start and end colours clearly in order.

exam.q: Give two observations you would see when excess zinc powder is added to dilute sulfuric acid.
model: Effervescence / bubbling / gas evolved
Zinc powder disappears / dissolves
exam.tip: Choose easily observable macroscopic changes like gas or solid disappearing.

exam.q: Explain why the temperature increases during a neutralisation reaction.
model: Neutralisation is an exothermic reaction
Thermal energy is released to the surroundings as bonds form
exam.tip: Use the keyword 'exothermic' for energy-releasing reactions.

exam.q: Write a full balanced equation with state symbols for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and solid magnesium oxide.
model: MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgCl2(aq) + H2O(l)
Correct formulas for reactants and products
Correct state symbols included
exam.tip: Check valencies: Magnesium is +2, Chloride is -1, so it is MgCl2.

worked.q: A student neutralises 25.0 cm3 of 0.200 mol/dm3 sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid. Calculate the moles of sodium hydroxide used.
steps: Recall formula: Moles = Concentration x Volume (in dm3).
Convert volume from cm3 to dm3: 25.0 / 1000 = 0.0250 dm3.
Calculate moles: 0.200 mol/dm3 x 0.0250 dm3 = 0.00500 moles.

worked.q: Identify the spectator ions in the reaction between aqueous potassium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid: KOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> KCl(aq) + H2O(l).
steps: Write out all aqueous species as separate ions: K+(aq) + OH-(aq) + H+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> K+(aq) + Cl-(aq) + H2O(l).
Locate which ions appear on both the reactant and product sides unchanged.
Potassium ions (K+) and chloride ions (Cl-) appear on both sides.
